# 30 Endoscopic Ultrasound of the Esophagus

## Overview 

**EUS**

- Combines **endoscopy** (flexible tube with light and camera) with **ultrasound technology**
- Visualizes internal organs and tissues in the **upper and lower GI tract**
- Evaluates:
  - Esophagus, stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum
  - Surrounding organs: pancreas, liver, lymph nodes
- Chapter focus: Basic principles of endosonography → EUS in the esophagus as it pertains to **esophageal cancer**



::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
- Key Advantage Over CT/MRI:

    - Potential to obtain **tissue samples** for histopathology and molecular testing
:::



---

### Principles of Endosonography: Fundamentals

**How Ultrasonography Works**

- Based on **high-frequency sound waves**
- Produced by applying voltage to a **transducer (piezoelectric crystal)**
- Sound waves transmitted through the GI tract lumen into the body

## Image Formation

1. Sound waves encounter **tissue boundaries** (e.g., solid organs vs. fluid-filled areas)
2. Waves are **reflected back** to the ultrasound probe
3. The **time** for round-trip + **strength** of reflected waves → creates the image

## Doppler Evaluation

- Measures **blood flow** through frequency change of the sound wave



## Echogenicity


The ability of a tissue to **reflect or transmit** ultrasound waves in the context of surrounding tissues.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
A visible contrast difference appears on screen whenever there is an interface of structures with different echogenicity.
:::

## Classification of Structures

| Term | Appearance | Examples |
|------|-----------|----------|
| **Hyperechoic** | White | Fat, air |
| **Hypoechoic** | Gray (darker) | Lymph nodes, tumors |
| **Isoechoic** | Same as surrounding | Difficult to distinguish |
| **Anechoic** | Black | Fluid-filled: cysts, arteries, veins |

## Clinical Pearl

Isoechoic lesions require identification through **subtleties in tissue interface**, shape, size, and location — a skill of the trained endosonographer.



## Types of Echoendoscopes: Radial {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
Radial EUS Endoscope

- **270–360°** ultrasonic probe at the tip
- Examines organs/lesions on the wall close to the GI tract
- Images are **perpendicular** to endoscope tip's axis
- **Cross-sectional orientation** — like an axial CT scan slice
- Best for examining **esophageal wall layers**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Typical Use

- Staging esophageal cancers
- Evaluating subepithelial lesions
- Anatomical landmark identification

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Often uses a **thin water-filled balloon** over the probe to improve contact
:::
:::

:::



## Types of Echoendoscopes: Linear

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
Linear Echoendoscope

- **100–180°** ultrasonic probe along one side of the tip
- Generates view **parallel** to the echoendoscope's shaft
- Optical viewing field is **oblique** (45–60° viewing angle)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Greatest Advantage

**Fine-Needle Aspiration / Biopsy (FNA/FNB)**

- Needle exits obliquely along the side of the probe
- Location and depth monitored under **ultrasound guidance**
- Enables tissue sampling **and** therapeutic interventions within the esophagus
:::

:::



## Radial vs. Linear: Comparison

| Feature | Radial | Linear |
|---------|--------|--------|
| **View angle** | 270–360° | 100–180° |
| **Image plane** | Perpendicular (cross-sectional) | Parallel to shaft |
| **Image orientation** | Like axial CT | Longitudinal |
| **FNA/FNB capability** | No | Yes |
| **Best use** | Wall layer assessment, anatomy | Tissue acquisition, interventions |
| **Balloon often used?** | Yes | No (usually unnecessary) |



## Imaging Artifacts in Esophageal EUS

**Common Challenge**: Tangential Imaging

- Occurs when transducer is at an angle **other than 90°** to the structure
- Leads to **overestimation** of object thickness
- Esophagus is particularly prone due to **wall compression** by the probe

**[Other Artifacts]{.underline}**

- Reverberation
- Mirror image
- Attenuation artifact



## Reducing Artifacts During Esophageal EUS

::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="50%"}
1. Water-Filled Balloon

- Thin balloon over the ultrasound probe fills with water
- Reduces **attenuation artifacts** from insufficient probe-wall contact
- Most often used during **radial** examinations
- Usually unnecessary for linear exams
::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
2. Water in the Esophageal Lumen

- Placed through the **biopsy channel** or via **air/water button**
- Improves acoustic coupling

::: {.callout-caution appearance="minimal"}
**Caution:** Risk of **aspiration** with high volumes — use water cautiously
:::
::::

:::



## Normal Anatomy: Five Layers of the Esophageal Wall

Knowing the layers is **vital** for staging esophageal cancers and evaluating subepithelial lesions.

| Layer | Echogenicity | Histologic Correlate |
|-------|--------------|----------------------|
| **1st** | Hyperechoic (white) | Interface between superficial mucosa and water |
| **2nd** | Hypoechoic (dark) | Deep mucosa |
| **3rd** | Hyperechoic (white) | Submucosa + acoustic interface with muscularis propria |
| **4th** | Hypoechoic (dark) | Muscularis propria |
| **5th** | Hyperechoic (white) | Outer adventitia (at esophageal level) |

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Best examined using a **radial echoendoscope**
:::



## Figure 30.1: Five Layers of the Esophageal Wall


**Key Layers**

- **m** = Mucosa
- **mm** = Muscularis mucosa
- **sm** = Submucosa
- **mp** = Muscularis propria
- **s** = Serosa


Five concentric alternating hyperechoic/hypoechoic rings



## Normal Anatomy: Radial Endosonography — Starting Point

**[Step-by-Step Approach]{.underline}**

1. Place radial echoendoscope at the **gastroesophageal junction (GEJ)**
2. **Inflate the balloon** on the radial echoendoscope
3. First structure seen: **aorta** (round, anechoic, confirmed with Doppler)
4. Use electronic rotation to place aorta at **5 o'clock position** (like a CT slice)
5. Ensure transducer is centered in the balloon
6. **Slowly withdraw** the scope



## Figure 30.2: Anatomical Landmarks at the GEJ

**Key Structures**

- **Aorta** positioned at 5 o'clock
- **IVC** (Inferior Vena Cava)
- **Liver** visible


Orientation mimics a **CT scan slice** for intuitive anatomical correlation



## Radial EUS: Mid-Esophageal Landmarks

[As the Scope is Withdrawn from GEJ]{.underline}

| Distance from Incisors | Landmark | Position |
|------------------------|----------|----------|
| **33–35 cm** | Left atrium | 10–12 o'clock |
| Just above LA | Subcarinal space | 12 o'clock (3–4 cm long) |
| **27–29 cm** | Left & right mainstem bronchi | 2 and 10 o'clock |

[Characteristics]{.underline}

- **Left atrium**: first major landmark after GEJ
- **Subcarinal space**: examine carefully for **lymph nodes**
- **Bronchi**: appear as **bright strands** due to air within them



## Figure 30.3: Left Atrium

**[Visible Structures]{.underline}**

- **Left Atrium**
- **Spine**
- **Aorta**
- **Subcarinal LN** (lymph node)


Typical location: **33–35 cm from incisors**

## Figure 30.4: Subcarinal Space

[**Key Features**]{.underline}

- Located at **12 o'clock**
- 3–4 cm in length
- Important site for **lymph node assessment**


Visible landmarks: Carina, Aortic Arch, Aorto-Pulmonary Window


## Radial EUS: Proximal Landmarks

Findings Over the Next 2–3 cm (after bronchi)

1. **Left and right mainstem bronchi** merge → form the **trachea** at 12 o'clock
2. **Azygous vein** joins the **superior vena cava**
3. **Elongation of aorta** → represents the **aortic arch**

Aortopulmonary Window (APW)

- Once aortic arch is identified, **advance scope 2–3 cm**
- APW located at **3 o'clock position**
- **Critical window** for identifying pathological lymph nodes



## Figure 30.5: Left and Right Mainstem Bronchi

[**Visible Structures**]{.underline}

- **Tracheal bifurcation**
- **Azygos arch**
- **Thoracic duct**
- **Aortic arch**


Bronchi appear as **bright strands** due to air



## Figure 30.6: Aorto-Pulmonary Window (Radial)

[**Key Features**]{.underline}

- Located at **3 o'clock**
- AA = Aortic Arch
- APW = Aorto-Pulmonary Window

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
Essential window for detecting **pathological lymph nodes**
:::



## Normal Anatomy: Linear Endosonography

- Why Linear is More Challenging

    - Plane of view is **parallel** to the endoscope axis
    - Less intuitive than radial EUS
    - Requires **in-depth anatomical knowledge** and optimal scope rotation

- General Approach

    1. After intubation, advance linear scope to the **GEJ**
    2. Begin examination during **withdrawal**
    3. Divided into: **distal, mid, and proximal** esophagus
    
## Normal Anatomy: Linear Endosonography

First Structure Identified

- **Descending thoracic aorta**
- Rotate **clockwise** → identify the **left atrium**
  - Appears as contracting chamber
  - Mitral valve opening into left ventricle visible



## Linear EUS: Mid-Esophageal Structures

With Continued Withdrawal

- **Ascending aorta** and **pulmonary artery** come into view
- Important for identifying **subcarinal lymph nodes** (Thoracic Node Station 7)

Continued Clockwise Rotation

- Brings the **superior vena cava** into view

Blind Spot

- Appears as scope is pulled over the **air-filled left mainstem bronchus**
- With rotation at this level:
  - **Arch of aorta** becomes visible
  - Just distal to arch: **cross-sectional view of right pulmonary artery**



## Figure 30.7: Subcarinal Space (Linear — Station 7)

Visible Structures

- **LA** = Left Atrium
- **LV** = Left Ventricle
- **PA** = Pulmonary artery

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Thoracic node **station 7** — critical for lung/esophageal cancer staging
:::



## Aortopulmonary Window (Linear — Station 5)

Location and Importance

- Between **aortic arch** and **right pulmonary artery**
- **Thoracic nodal station 5**
- Malignant mediastinal lymph nodes often identified here

Proximal Esophagus / Neck Withdrawal

- **Trachea** anteriorly
- **Spine** posteriorly
- Vascular structures:
  - Left common carotid
  - Right common carotid
  - Deep internal jugular veins



## Figure 30.8: Aorto-Pulmonary Window (Linear — Station 5)

Visible Structures

- **PA** = Pulmonary Artery
- **APW** = Aorto-Pulmonary Window
- **Aortic arch**

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
Critical for staging mediastinal lymphadenopathy
:::



## Linear EUS: Azygous Vein Tracking

Returning to Distal Esophagus

- Identify the **azygous vein**
- **Rotate counterclockwise** from descending aorta → azygous vein comes into view
- **Withdraw scope while tracking** the azygous vein
- Reveals the **superior vena cava**

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Useful technique to map the posterior mediastinal vascular anatomy
:::



## Indications for EUS of the Esophagus

- EUS is both a **diagnostic** and **therapeutic** tool with a wide variety of indications.

- Primary Roles in the Esophagus

    - **Local staging** of esophageal cancer
    - Evaluation and sampling of **subepithelial lesions**
    - Evaluation of **posterior mediastinal lesions**
    - Assessment of **paraoesophageal / posterior mediastinal adenopathy**

## Additional Applications (beyond this chapter)

- Esophageal subepithelial lesions
- Mediastinal masses and lymphadenopathy
- Lung cancer staging

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
**Chapter Focus:** Role of EUS in esophageal cancer
:::



## EUS vs. CT in T-Staging

Diagnostic Accuracy Comparison

| Modality | T-Staging Accuracy |
|----------|-------------------|
| **CT Scan** | 45% |
| **EUS** | 85% |

*Based on systematic review data*

## Additional Advantages of EUS

- Allows **tissue acquisition (FNA)** of nodal structures in and around the esophagus
- Superior for locoregional staging

## Requirements for Accurate Evaluation

- Excellent understanding of **esophageal and periesophageal anatomy**
- Knowledge of **staging classifications**
- Basic understanding of **EUS techniques** and **image interpretation**



## Esophageal Cancer Staging: AJCC System

TNM Classification

Esophageal cancer staging uses the **American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC)** system:

| Component | Definition |
|--------|-----------|
| **T** | Depth of invasion of the primary tumor |
| **N** | Lymph node involvement |
| **M** | Extent of metastatic disease |

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
The TNM components are **the same** for esophageal **adenocarcinoma** and **squamous cell carcinoma**
:::



## Tumor (T) Staging: Overview

| Stage | Depth of Invasion |
|-------|-------------------|
| **T1a** | Mucosa (lamina propria or muscularis mucosae) |
| **T1b** | Submucosa |
| **T2** | Muscularis propria (4th hypoechoic layer) |
| **T3** | Through muscularis propria → adventitia |
| **T4** | Through adventitia → adjacent structures |



## T1a Tumor: Confined to Mucosa

Definition

- Cancerous involvement **limited to the mucosa**
- Invades into the **lamina propria** or **muscularis mucosae**

Clinical Significance

- **<5% risk** of nodal metastasis
- Can be treated with **endoscopic resection**



## T1b Tumor: Submucosal Invasion

Definition

- Invasion extends into the **submucosa**

Clinical Significance

- **15–30% rate** of lymph node metastasis
- Treated with **surgical resection**

## Distinguishing T1a from T1b

- **Critical distinction** for treatment planning
- Meta-analysis: EUS sensitivity of **85%** for distinguishing T1a vs T1b
- Some debate exists regarding EUS accuracy in early disease (risk of overstaging)



## T2 Tumor: Muscularis Propria Invasion

Definition

- Tumor invades the **muscularis propria**
- Corresponds to the **4th hypoechoic layer** seen on EUS

Clinical Relevance

- Detection of suspicious lymph nodes can **change treatment course**, especially for T2 disease
- Accurate staging determines need for neoadjuvant therapy





## T3 Tumor: Adventitial Invasion

Definition

- Tumor invades **through the muscularis propria**
- Involves the **adventitia**

Imaging Features

- Disruption of the 4th hypoechoic layer
- Extension into the 5th hyperechoic layer (adventitia)





## T4 Tumor: Adjacent Structure Invasion

Definition

- Tumor invades **through the adventitia**
- Involves **adjacent structures** (e.g., aorta, trachea, pericardium)

Clinical Significance

- Generally considered **unresectable**
- Requires multimodal therapy approach



## Nodal (N) Staging

Definition

- Nodal stage determined by the **number of lymph nodes involved**

Prognostic Significance

| Malignant Lymph Nodes | Median Survival |
|----------------------|-----------------|
| **0 nodes** | 66 months |
| **>2 nodes** | 6.5 months |


Clinical Impact

- Detection of suspicious nodes can **change treatment course**
- Especially impactful for patients with **T2 disease**

::: {.callout-caution appearance="minimal"}
Number of positive lymph nodes **directly correlates** with decreased survival
:::


## EUS Features of Malignant Lymph Nodes

Four Key Features

1. **Size > 1 cm**
2. **Round shape**
3. **Clearly demarcated borders**
4. **Hypoechoic**

Predictive Value

| Number of Features Present | Probability of Metastatic Involvement |
|---------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Some features | ~80% |
| **All 4 features** | **80–100%** |



## N-Staging: EUS Accuracy

Comparative Accuracy

| Modality | Accuracy for N-Staging |
|----------|------------------------|
| **Helical CT** | 51% |
| **EUS alone** | 74% |
| **EUS + FNA** | 87% |

*Based on prospective study data*

## Limitations of EUS-FNA for Lymph Nodes

- Potential **seeding risk**
- Added **time and cost**
- **Inability to sample nodes through tumor**

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Authors' practice:** FNA of suspicious-appearing lymph nodes is **not routinely performed**
:::



## Distant Metastasis (M) Staging

Definition

Spread of tumor **outside of regional lymph nodes**

Common Sites of Distant Metastasis

| Site | Frequency |
|------|-----------|
| **Liver** | 33.4% |
| **Distant (nonregional) lymph nodes** | 26.6% |
| **Lung** | 20.5% |
| **Bone** | 15.7% |
| **Brain** | 3.8% |

**Role of EUS in M-Staging**: **Limited** for detecting metastatic disease



## M-Staging: Imaging Modality Comparison

Accuracy for Distant Metastasis Detection

| Modality | Accuracy |
|----------|----------|
| **PET** | 86% |
| **Combined CT + EUS** | 62% |

NCCN Recommendations

1. **CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis** at time of cancer diagnosis
2. If no overt distant metastatic disease on CT:
   - **Both EUS and PET** recommended for additional examination

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
**PET is superior** to combined CT + EUS for detecting distant metastases
:::



## Role of EUS in Obstructing Tumors {.smaller}

#### The Challenge

- **20–36%** of esophageal cancers prevent passage of the echoendoscope
- Due to **high-grade malignant strictures**
- Inability to pass the scope **limits accurate T and N staging**

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Staging accuracy is **much higher** in traversable vs. nontraversable cancers
:::



## Overcoming Obstructing Tumor Limitations: Method 1

#### Limited EUS Staging Proximal to the Stricture

**Approach:**

- Perform staging examination only above the stricture
- May be a **safe alternative** to esophageal dilation

**Limitations:**

- Accuracy only **28%**
- Lymph node assessment **distal** to the lesion is limited
- Cannot visualize the **celiac axis**



## Overcoming Obstructing Tumor Limitations: Method 2

#### Dilation of the Stricture

**Goal:** Allow passage of the 12–13 mm diameter echoendoscope

**Outcomes:**

- Success rate of passing EUS scope: **33%** (standard dilation)
- **87%** success when dilated to 14–16 mm (2000 study)
- Only **33%** had accurate preoperative assessment of tumor depth after dilation

**Risks:**

- Esophageal perforation risk: **up to 24%**



## Overcoming Obstructing Tumor Limitations: Method 3

#### High-Frequency Catheter Ultrasonic Probes (HFCP) / Mini Probes

**Advantages:**

- Small diameter (**3 mm**) → may pass beyond stenotic lumen
- Detailed examination of esophageal wall possible

**Limitations:**

- Higher frequency (**20 MHz**) → limited depth of penetration
- **Poor accuracy** for N-staging
- **Cannot discriminate** between T3 and T4 tumors
- Not routinely used in clinical practice



## Authors' Approach to Obstructing Tumors

::: {.callout-caution appearance="minimal"}
**Dilation of obstructing tumors is NOT regularly performed** in the authors' practice
:::

#### Rationale

1. **Risk of perforation**
2. Detailed information obtainable from **CT and PET scans**
3. Obstructing tumors are usually at least **T3 stage**
4. Require **neoadjuvant chemotherapy** regardless

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
Clinical decision-making often proceeds without full EUS staging in obstructing tumors
:::



## Role of EUS After Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy

#### The Controversy

Role of EUS after neoadjuvant chemoradiation (CRT) is **controversial** because treatment causes:

- **Inflammation**
- **Fibrosis**
- **Necrosis**

→ Leads to **hypoechoic appearance** of the esophageal wall

→ Limits EUS ability to **accurately differentiate wall layers**



## EUS Accuracy After Neoadjuvant Therapy

#### Study Findings

| Outcome | EUS Accuracy |
|---------|--------------|
| Correctly identifying **complete response** to CRT | **27%** |
| Tumor and nodal staging accuracy **after chemotherapy** | **60%** |

::: {.callout-caution appearance="minimal"}
**Limited sensitivity** → EUS after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is **not common practice** at the authors' center
:::

#### Implication

- Poor ability to **downstage** disease accurately
- Treatment decisions post-CRT rely on other modalities



## Conclusion

#### Key Takeaways

::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="50%"}
#### EUS as a Tool

- **Powerful tool** for diagnosis and staging of esophageal cancer
- **Linear endoscopes** expanded the role:
  - Accurate visualization
  - Tissue acquisition (FNA/FNB)
  - Accurate diagnosis and locoregional staging
::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
#### Clinical Impact

- Data obtained by EUS has **meaningful and significant impact** on medical and surgical management
- Beyond esophageal cancer:
  - Subepithelial lesions
  - Mediastinal masses & lymphadenopathy
  - Lung cancer
::::

:::

## Future Directions

- Since introduction, **advances in technology and techniques** have dramatically expanded applications
- Evolution from **diagnostic → interventional EUS**
- Expected to continue emerging as an **invaluable tool** in esophageal disease management



## Summary Table: Key EUS Applications in Esophageal Cancer

| Application | Role of EUS | Accuracy / Notes |
|-------------|-------------|------------------|
| **T-staging** | Excellent | 85% accuracy (vs 45% CT) |
| **N-staging** | Very good | 87% with FNA |
| **M-staging** | Limited | PET is superior (86% vs 62%) |
| **T1a vs T1b distinction** | Good | 85% sensitivity |
| **Post-neoadjuvant restaging** | Poor | 27–60% accuracy |
| **Obstructing tumors** | Challenging | Consider CT/PET instead |
